Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service San Diego CA
1149 AM PST Thu Nov 26 2026

.SYNOPSIS...
Coastal flooding is expected to continue into Friday due to King 
Tides and elevated to high surf. Warmer today and Friday with 
highs 10 to 15 degrees above normal and breezy offshore winds. 
Cooling will spread inland Saturday through Wednesday. There is a
50 percent chance for showers from the coast to the mountains 
Sunday night and Monday. Chances for moderate to heavy rainfall 
and high elevation mountain snow increase significantly Tuesday 
and Wednesday as a strong Pacific storm moves inland into 
California.

&&

.DISCUSSION...FOR EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA INCLUDING ORANGE...
SAN DIEGO...WESTERN RIVERSIDE AND SOUTHWESTERN SAN BERNARDINO
COUNTIES...

Morning water vapor imagery shows an upper level ridge of high
pressure building in from the west. At the surface, pressure
gradioents peaked earlier this morning at -6.2 mb SAN-DAG,
currently down to -5.6 mb SAN-DAG. This is producing northeast to
east winds gusting to 25-40 mph below the passes, canyons, and
coastal mountain slopes. Winds will gradually weaken through the
afternoon with light offshore flow continuing into Friday morning,
transitioning to a sea breeze in the afternoon. The upper level
ridge moving overhead into Friday combined with weak offshore flow
will generate warm conditions across the region. Widespread highs
in the low to mid 80s are expected across the coastal areas,
valleys, and low deserts both days, warmest on Friday. Highs in
the mountains will be in the low 60s to low 70s, and mid 60s to
low 70s in the high desert.

The upper level ridge breaks down in response to an upper low
moving across the top of it and into the Pac NW this weekend,
allowing for gradual cooling and a return of onshore flow, though
high temperatures remain several degrees above normal. Otherwise
just expect some scattered to broken high clouds at times this
weekend.

Precipitable water increases to around 0.8" on Monday as upper
level zonal flow ushers in some subtropical moisture. However,
only weak, very subtle short waves will be moving through the mean
flow, providing little if any forcing for precipitation. Current
forecast has a 25-45% chance of precipitation for the mountains
westward on Monday, but any accumulation will likely be limited to
one-tenth inch or less. 

A deep long wave trough is then forecast to move through
California Tuesday into Wednesday, bringing gusty southwest to
west winds and widespread precipitation to the region. There
remains differences in the ensembles with regards to how far south
this trough will dig, as well as the timing. The more significant
spread lies in the forecast Integrated Vapor Transport (IVT). The
GEFS and EPS 10th to 90th percentiles of IVT range from about 150
to over 600 kg/m/s, so anywhere from too low to be considered an
Atmospheric River to a moderate AR. This is likely the main cause
of the large spread in forecast rainfall from this system. The NBM
25th percentile 48 hr precipitation currently ranges from about
1.5-2" for the mountains westward, up to 2.5" on the coastal
slopes of the mountains, while the 75th percentile is around
2.3-3" for the mountains westward, and 3.5-4" on the coastal
mountain slopes. While it is far too early to nail down specific
rainfall totals, this is leaning towards a moderate to heavy rain
event. Potential snow levels range from around 6500 ft in a colder
scenario event to as high as 8000 ft on the warmer end. Weak
instability (surface based CAPE of 100-200 J/kg) will produce a
slight chance of thunderstorms Tue-Wed as well, mainly over the
coastal waters into the valleys. Light showers could persist into
Thursday (10-20% chance).

&&

.AVIATION... 
261800Z...VFR prevailing with SKC. Northeast winds with gusts 25-35 
kts along coastal slopes and through passes, decreasing around 22z. 
SCT-BKN high clouds AOA 20kft moves in this evening/early Friday 
morning with lighter winds.

&&

.MARINE...
Combined seas of 7 to 10 feet in the outer coastal waters south of 
San Clemente Island will continue through the morning. Seas lower 
this afternoon, falling below 8 feet by this evening.

&&

.BEACHES...
The La Jolla tide gauge recorded a high tide of 8.11 ft MLLW 
Wednesday morning, preliminarily breaking the all-time record just 
recently set on October 27th. King Tides continue today, and have 
peaked just below 8 ft this morning. Forecast tides have been 
adjusted 1.1-1.2 feet above baseline astronomical predictions based 
on trends in recent observations. 

A long period west swell of 7-9 ft at 16-18 seconds is generating 
large breaking waves of 6-8 feet, with sets of 10-12 feet on exposed 
west-facing beaches. Surf lowers to 3-5 feet with local sets to 7 
feet on Friday. A High Surf Advisory is in effect for San Diego 
County through 4 AM Friday with the swell focusing the higher surf 
on the west-facing beaches.

The combination of forecast record King Tides and elevated to high 
surf will bring moderate to major coastal flooding, with locally 
extreme flooding expected during this morning's high tide. A Coastal 
Flood Warning remains in effect through early Friday afternoon.

&&

.SKYWARN... 
Skywarn activation is not requested. However weather spotters are
encouraged to report significant weather conditions.


&&

     Coastal Areas.
